scenes.title: Foundation: quadratic forms and signs
scenes.objective: Recall symmetric matrices, eigenvalues and definiteness.

ask.q: What is the quadratic form associated with a symmetric matrix A?
ask.nudge: It is a scalar formed from x transpose, A and x.

body: A quadratic form in x is Q(x)=xᵀAx, where A is a real symmetric matrix. For two variables it has the form ax²+2bxy+cy².
The factor 2 on the cross-term matters: xᵀ[[a,b],[b,c]]x=ax²+2bxy+cy². Any real quadratic form can be represented by a symmetric matrix, since the antisymmetric part contributes zero to xᵀAx.

items.recall: Q(x)>0 for every non-zero real vector x.
refresh: The strict inequality applies to every non-zero vector. At x=0 the form is necessarily zero, so zero is excluded from the definition.

For a real symmetric matrix, positive definiteness is equivalent to all eigenvalues being strictly positive. It is also equivalent to positivity of all leading principal minors by Sylvester's criterion.

For a 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[b,c]], the determinant ac−b² is only one part of the test: positive definiteness requires a>0 as well as ac−b²>0. This prevents a negative definite matrix from being misclassified just because its determinant is positive.

items.recall: The determinant of a submatrix formed by selecting the same index set for rows and columns.
refresh: A leading principal minor uses the first k rows and first k columns. For a 3×3 matrix, the leading minors have orders 1, 2 and 3.
Sylvester's criterion uses leading principal minors, not every arbitrary minor. Confusing these tests is a common exam trap.

items.ask: What is an eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix?
items.recall: A scalar λ for which Av=λv for some non-zero vector v.
refresh: Real symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis. This makes eigenvalues a direct test of the signs of the quadratic form.
Under an orthogonal change of coordinates, a symmetric quadratic form becomes a sum of eigenvalue-weighted squares. The signs of those coefficients determine definiteness.

scenes.title: A quadratic surface has a signature
scenes.objective: Interpret positive, negative and mixed curvature.

ask.q: What does Q(x,y)=x²−4y² tell you about the sign of the form?

body: A positive definite form is bowl-shaped: it is positive in every non-zero direction. A negative definite form is the same shape turned upside down.

An indefinite form has both positive and negative directions. For x²−4y², the x-axis gives a positive value and the y-axis a negative value. A semidefinite form allows zero along some non-zero directions but never changes sign.

ask.q: A symmetric matrix has eigenvalues 4, 1 and 0. Classify its quadratic form.
ask.nudge: All eigenvalues are non-negative, but one is zero.

blocks.body: Positive definite: all λᵢ>0. Positive semidefinite: all λᵢ≥0. Negative definite: all λᵢ<0. Negative semidefinite: all λᵢ≤0. Indefinite: at least one positive and one negative eigenvalue.
A zero eigenvalue rules out strict definiteness. If the remaining eigenvalues are all positive, the form is positive semidefinite; if signs are mixed, it is indefinite.
The inertia is the triple (p,n,z): number of positive, negative and zero eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity. It is invariant under nonsingular congruence transformations.

scenes.title: Sylvester's criterion
scenes.objective: Use leading principal minors to test definiteness.

ask.q: For a 3×3 symmetric matrix, what signs must its three leading principal minors have for positive definiteness?
ask.nudge: They must all be strictly positive.

blocks.body: A real symmetric A is positive definite iff Δ₁>0, Δ₂>0, …, Δₙ>0, where Δₖ is the kth leading principal minor.
A is negative definite iff (−1)ᵏΔₖ>0 for every k. For order 3 the signs are Δ₁<0, Δ₂>0, Δ₃<0.

blocks.h: Do not use the wrong minors
blocks.body: The criterion uses leading principal minors in the fixed top-left sequence. Checking only det(A), or checking every principal minor without understanding the theorem, is not the intended shortcut.

scenes.title: Worked: a 2×2 classification
scenes.objective: Classify a quadratic form using its matrix and minors.

ask.q: For A=[[2,1],[1,2]], what are Δ₁, Δ₂ and the definiteness?

steps.why: The cross-term 2xy means the off-diagonal entries are both 1.
Both required leading minors are strictly positive.
For a real symmetric 2×2 matrix, Δ₁>0 and Δ₂>0 are necessary and sufficient.

scenario.teaser: A covariance-like quadratic penalty must never be negative.
scenario.title: Positive definiteness in a least-squares penalty
body: A quadratic penalty xᵀAx is used to measure the cost of a parameter displacement. If A is positive definite, every non-zero displacement has strictly positive cost.
If A is only positive semidefinite, some non-zero directions have zero cost. These are flat directions and may signal an unidentified or unpenalised component.
The matrix must be symmetric for the standard real quadratic-form interpretation. The definiteness check is therefore a structural diagnostic, not just a determinant exercise.

The same reasoning applies to regularisation penalties and covariance matrices, although a covariance matrix is naturally positive semidefinite rather than necessarily positive definite when variables are linearly dependent.

scenes.title: Canonical reduction by orthogonal transformation
scenes.objective: Reduce a symmetric form to a sum of weighted squares.

ask.q: If A is real symmetric, what transformation diagonalises it while preserving Euclidean lengths?

blocks.body: A=QΛQᵀ, where QᵀQ=I and Λ=diag(λ₁,…,λₙ). With y=Qᵀx, Q(x)=yᵀΛy=Σλᵢyᵢ².

Orthogonal transformations are invertible coordinate changes. They rotate or reflect axes but do not collapse directions. The diagonal coefficients therefore expose the positive, negative and zero directions.

A and PᵀAP are congruent for nonsingular P. Sylvester's law of inertia says their counts of positive, negative and zero squares are identical, even though the numerical eigenvalues need not be identical under general congruence.

scenes.title: Guided: reduce a diagonal form
scenes.objective: Read inertia and definiteness from a canonical expression.
hints: The diagonal coefficients are already the eigenvalues of the diagonal matrix.
Count positive, negative and zero coefficients separately.
There is one of each sign category; the form takes both positive and negative values.

solution.say: The coefficients are 3, −2 and 0. There is one positive square, one negative square and one zero square. Since both positive and negative directions occur, the form is indefinite.

ask.q: Can a form with inertia (2,0,1) be positive definite?
ask.nudge: A zero direction prevents strict positivity.

scenes.title: Principal minors: semidefinite caution
scenes.objective: Avoid applying strict Sylvester signs to semidefinite forms.

ask.q: Is diag(2,0) positive definite or positive semidefinite?

blocks.body: For positive semidefinite matrices, every principal minor (not merely the leading ones) must be non-negative. For negative semidefinite, principal minors of order k must have sign (−1)ᵏ or be zero.
Sylvester's strict leading-minor criterion is the fast test for positive or negative definiteness. It cannot simply be changed to ≥0 to test semidefiniteness; all principal minors matter.
A=[[0,1],[1,0]] has leading minors Δ₁=0 and Δ₂=−1. It is indefinite, with eigenvalues 1 and −1. Non-negative leading minors alone would not certify semidefiniteness.

scenes.title: Guided: apply Sylvester's criterion
scenes.problem: A symmetric matrix has leading principal minors Δ₁=2, Δ₂=3 and Δ₃=5.
hints: Write down all three signs before naming the class.
All three leading minors are strictly positive.
Apply Sylvester's criterion for positive definiteness.

solution.say: Since Δ₁=2>0, Δ₂=3>0 and Δ₃=5>0, Sylvester's criterion gives positive definiteness.

ask.q: If instead Δ₁<0, Δ₂>0 and Δ₃<0, what is the class?
ask.nudge: For order 3, these are the alternating signs for negative definiteness.

items.a: All leading principal minors are strictly positive.

items.q: What does Sylvester's law of inertia preserve?
items.a: The counts of positive, negative and zero squares under nonsingular congruence.

scenes.title: The geometry behind inertia
scenes.objective: Connect inertia with the shape of level sets.

ask.q: What does one positive and one negative eigenvalue produce in two dimensions?

body: For Q(x)=1, a positive definite form produces an ellipsoid in higher dimensions. A negative definite form has no real points at positive level 1, while an indefinite form produces hyperboloid-type geometry.
Zero eigenvalues create flat directions. In statistics these may correspond to non-identifiable directions or redundant variables. The inertia is the coordinate-free summary of these directions.

scenario.teaser: A flat direction appears in a quadratic penalty.
scenario.title: A zero eigenvalue as an unpenalised direction
body: Suppose a model uses Q(β)=βᵀAβ as a penalty. If A is positive definite, every non-zero coefficient displacement incurs a positive penalty.

If A is positive semidefinite with a zero eigenvalue, there is a non-zero direction v with Av=0 and vᵀAv=0. Moving along that direction does not change the penalty, so the quadratic form has a flat direction.

This can be intentional, as in a penalty that leaves an intercept unpenalised, or it can reveal redundancy. The inertia (p,n,z) reports how many positive, negative and flat directions exist, independent of the nonsingular coordinate change used to describe the parameters.

scenes.title: Worked: determinant is not enough
scenes.objective: Show why a positive determinant alone does not imply positive definiteness.

ask.q: For A=[[−1,0],[0,−2]], determinant is positive. Is the form positive definite?
ask.nudge: Check the first leading principal minor.

steps.say: Check the first leading principal minor.
steps.why: The sign of the first minor distinguishes positive from negative definiteness.

steps.math: det(A)>0 alone does not determine definiteness.
steps.why: For 2×2 matrices, positive determinant means eigenvalues have the same sign; trace or the first minor distinguishes their sign.

scenes.title: Trap check: six statements
scenes.objective: Identify common errors in definiteness tests.
scenes.intro: Judge each statement true or false.

items.claim: A positive definite matrix has all positive eigenvalues.
items.why: For real symmetric matrices this is equivalent to positive definiteness.

items.claim: A positive determinant guarantees positive definiteness.
items.why: A negative definite 2×2 matrix can have a positive determinant.

items.claim: Sylvester's strict criterion uses leading principal minors.
items.why: All leading principal minors must be strictly positive.

items.claim: For semidefiniteness, checking only leading principal minors is sufficient in general.
items.why: All principal minors must be non-negative.

items.claim: Inertia is invariant under nonsingular congruence.
items.why: This is Sylvester's law of inertia.

items.claim: An indefinite form takes both positive and negative values.
items.why: That is the defining sign behaviour.

scenes.title: Your final definiteness checklist
scenes.objective: Choose the right test without mixing the criteria.
body: 1. Write Q(x)=xᵀAx using a symmetric A; halve the displayed cross-term to obtain off-diagonal entries.
2. If eigenvalues are available, count their positive, negative and zero signs.
3. For positive definite: all leading principal minors >0.
4. For negative definite: (−1)^kΔ_k>0 for every k.
5. For semidefinite: use all principal minors with the appropriate non-strict signs.
6. For canonical reduction, use orthogonal diagonalisation for real symmetric A; inertia is preserved by nonsingular congruence.
